about: The words of the chain lindisfarne_book (Data/encounters/chain_lindisfarne_book_793.json; Design/content/chains/lindisfarne_book.md): a gospel book carried off from Lindisfarne on 8 June 793 and seen for sale in the north. Every title, intention, line and label key of its thirteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items the endings post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Bishop Higbald, Bishop Ecgberht, Archbishop Eanbald, Alcuin and Abbot Gervold are historical; Thorleif, Asulf, Holmfast, Sigewine, the lookout Beornwine and the steersman Aldger are the spine's cast; Ketil the dealer, Gunnhild, the scribe Eadwulf and Wigfrith who wrote the book are ordinary invented people. The book itself is invented: a lesser gospel book of the house, not the great Gospels. Nothing here is quoted from any translation: all of it is our own plain wording. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A strip of gilt

On a dealer's cloth, between a cup and a little box shaped like a house, lies a strip of gilt bronze worked in knots, with four rivet holes and no rivets. It was made to be fastened to something flat.
Western work. A man came home from over the sea with a chest of it, and none of it any use on a farm. I buy what the women do not want.
That strip came off a board. The board was the lid of a block of calfskins, sewn at one edge, with small black marks on every skin and pictures on some. He broke the gold off and kept the skins.
The round piece with the stone in it his wife took, and had a pin put on the back. The women like the knots. The men ask what it weighs.
He showed the skins here at the end of summer. Nobody bid. What would a man do with them? But he would not burn them either. He lives west, on the sound where the ships go north.
Buy the strip for twelve pennies' weight
Leave the strip and ask where the skins went
Sit down with him over ale, in his own tongue
He weighs your silver against a lead weight, twice, and wraps the strip in a dock leaf. It is lighter than it looks. Whoever made it took a month over a thing no wider than two fingers.
West, he says again, on the Karmsund: a hall on the point, and a big man with red in his beard. He does not say the name, and you do not think he has forgotten it.

By the second horn he has said it. Thorleif, at Ögvaldsnes. He wants swords and a second ship, and has no use for prayers. 'He calls it a good landing. He had four men to bury after it, so judge what he calls a bad one.'
What is gone
The bishop stands in a church with its doors off and counts on his fingers what the heathen men took. He has done it before; he does not need to think.
The silver from the shrine. Two cups and the plate of the altar. The cloths. The brethren they killed. The boys they took. And a gospel book.

Not the great book. That one they did not find, God be thanked. The book of the daily altar, that went out to the sick and round the fields on the Rogation days. Wigfrith wrote it, in Bishop Æthelwold's time.

You would know it. On the first leaf of John there is a hole in the skin the size of a pea, where the calf had a scar, and Wigfrith wrote round it. On the last leaf he asks a prayer for himself, by name.
He turns the strip over twice. 'This was on the lower edge of the front board. I have had my thumb on it every Easter since they made me bishop. Where did you buy it? No. Tell me slowly.'
You have seen a piece of it? In a market, on a cloth, beside a cup. Yes. That is how it would be.
The boys first, if you hear of them. I have their names. Alcuin writes that he will speak to King Charles for them. A book does not lie awake at night. But ask after the book also.

I cannot pay as a king pays. Wax, some wine when we have it, what silver they left, and what our estates send at the feasts. And the saint does not forget who served him. That is not nothing, on this coast.
Say you will keep your eyes open in the north
Put the gilt strip in his hand
Ask what the altar is short of, and take his order for wine

He nods as a man nods who has been promised things all summer. Then he tells you the boys' names, one finger each, and makes you say them back. At Eoforwic, he says, a scribe of the minster can tell you what such a book is worth, so that you are not cheated in either direction.

He will not give the strip back, and you had not thought he would. A brother brings a cake of wax down to the boat: it is what the house has today. The bishop walks with you as far as the sand and tells you the marks of the book again.

Four casks of Rhine wine, for the altar and for the sick, before the second winter. The price will come from the house's farms on the mainland, and it is a good one. He tells you the marks of the book while a brother cuts the tally.
A herd of calves
In the minster's writing room a scribe hears your errand from the island without looking up, finishes his line, wipes the pen and then tells you what a book is.
A gospel book is a herd of calves. A hundred skins for a middling one, more for a great one, and each skin scraped, stretched and ruled before a word goes on it.

Then a year of a man's eyes. Then the colours, which come further than you do. So: to its own house it is worth whatever the house has. To another church, a farm. To a heathen, the weight of its mounts.
That is your luck, if you find it. He will have sold the gold already and will think the rest is rubbish. Do not correct him until you have paid.
Alcuin's letter to the king was read here before the whole household. We made copies. It says the sack of Saint Cuthbert's church is a judgement on us. The king did not enjoy it.
You are a Frisian. Frisians are remembered in this city. I would not stand long by that window.
And shut the door. The cold is in my thumb. Nobody writes that at the end of a book, but every book has it in it.
Stay three days and learn to tell a gospel book from a psalter
Take the writing room's order for colours
Ask only for a copy of Alcuin's letter, to show whose errand you are on

Three days on a bench with books you may not touch. By the end you know the four beasts of the four gospels, where each book begins, and what the red letters are for. He sends you off with a riddle about a thing that was killed, soaked, scraped and dressed in gold, and says a merchant ought to get it in one.

Red lead, the yellow that looks like gold, and the green if you can get it dry: he cuts the order on a tally and gives you a copy of Alcuin's letter to wrap it in. 'Read it if you can. If you cannot, carry it as if you could.'

He gives you a copy from the pile without a word and goes back to his line. At the door he says, to the page and not to you, that the first leaf of John is where a liar's book and a true one part company.
The hole in the page
The English lookout has been quiet for a day, which is not like him. At the evening meal he says he has seen the book you are asking after.
I was nine. My brother was given to the island and we went up with him for the feast. They carried it round the fields, and he was let hold the cloth it lay on. He was sick with pride.
There is a hole in one leaf. The scribe wrote round it, like a stream round a stone. The brothers showed it to all the new boys. It was the only joke in the house.
If we find it: a wet book is a ruined book. The skins swell and the colours run. In this boat there is one dry place, under the stern board, and it has your spare boots in it.
They took him too. He was twelve. I do not ask you to look for him. I only say that the book and the boy went in the same ship.
Have him sew a sealskin wrap and clear the dry place under the stern board
Have him teach you the first words of John, to test any book you are shown
Tell him a lookout looks at the sea

He sews it double, hair side in, rubbed with tallow, with a flap that folds twice. Your boots go forward with everyone else's. The steersman says the boat has a chapel now and asks who is to sweep it.

'In principio erat verbum.' He makes you say it until it stops sounding like a cough, and draws the shape of the great first letter on his wax tablet. Now you can find the leaf yourself, in any house, with nobody's help.
He goes forward and looks at the sea. He looks at it very thoroughly for two days and reports every gull.
A box of skins
A big red-fair man has a thing to show to anyone who trades with Christians: a block of sewn calfskins without boards, the first leaf a page of knots in red, yellow and green.
We had a good landing once, west over the sea. A low island, a house full of men who do not fight. This was in it.
Ketil talks. I knew a Frisian would come asking before the Frisian did.
The gold I took off. The skins I kept. Look at that: a man made that with a feather. I have a smith who could not do it with a chisel.
You turn straight to one leaf and put your finger through a hole in it. So it is the one you want, and you know it is. That was honest of your finger. It has cost you the haggling.
You turn the leaves like a man looking for something and not finding it. One box of skins looks much like another, they tell me. This is the one I have.
The woman at the loom wears a round gilt mount on her cloak, with a clear stone in the middle. She sees you look. 'It was on the lid. He says the lid was ugly. It was not.'
Two swords, Frankish, with the hilts on. Or silver in the scale until I say stop, and I stop at about the weight of a good axe head. Not prayers. I was offered prayers on the island, loudly.
It sleeps in the chest by my bed, and my hounds sleep on the chest. I say so because some guests are forgetful.
Weigh him out three hundred pennies of silver
Give him two Frankish swords for it
Tell him what it is and whose, and leave it on his chest
Say nothing, and come back for it after dark

The pennies go into his scale as plain metal; he does not look at the king's name on them. When the pan drops he says stop, and laughs, and adds one more with his own finger. The book goes down to your boat in a flour sack.

He draws each blade, bends it against his knee, and listens to it. Then he puts the book in your arms himself, as a man hands over a child he was minding. 'I hope your god reads better than I do.' You do not ask where the swords will go next summer.

You tell him: it is the word of the Christians' god, written for one house, and that house would give more for it than any market. He hears you out. 'Then it will not go for skins. I will send it south with the autumn lot and see who weeps most.' He has ale brought, and it is good ale.

The hounds know your smell from the afternoon and the man sleeps like the just. You are at sea before the tide turns, with the book between your feet. Behind you a horn blows once, and then for a long time.

The hounds are quiet until your hand is on the lid. His men throw you down the beach and your crew after you. He does not kill a guest, he says, but he may improve one. From the door he calls that the skins go south to Asulf with the autumn lot, if you would like to try buying next time.
Green water
The wind backs and hardens in the afternoon. The steersman looks at the sky to windward and then at the bundle of calfskins in the bottom of the boat.
She will take water over the quarter before dark. That is the worst of it. The rest is only work. Say now where the skins ride.
The boy's sealskin is tight; I tried it with a bucket. Under the stern board it will be drier than I am.
A flour sack keeps out flour. If we drive her, the sea chooses. If we lie to, you choose, and we lose the day.
Shorten sail, lie to, and hold it on your knees under the tilt until it blows through
It rides in the sealskin under the stern board: sail on
Wedge it under the thwart with the spare sail over it and drive on

A night with the sail down and the book in your lap, like a man nursing a goose. By morning the wind has gone round and the skins are dry. The crew have a new name for you and use it only among themselves.
Twice the sea comes in green over the quarter and runs out through the bailing. When it is over the lookout opens the flap with clean hands. Dry as a bone. He is unbearable about it for a week.
She takes one sea aboard and shakes it off. The sail over the bundle is wet through, and under it the sack is only damp at one corner. The steersman says nothing, which from him is praise.

The third sea fills her to the thwarts. When you can look, the bundle has been lying in water. The leaves at one edge are swollen and the green has run on the pages of Mark. It is still a book. It is not the book it was this morning.
The same square sail
A sail lifts astern at first light and does not fall behind. By mid morning there are shields along her side and a big man standing in her bow, in no hurry.
Striped, red and undyed. I know that sail. I have known it since I was told of it. Blessed is the man... no. I cannot think of the rest.
Frisian! You left in the night and forgot to pay. I came to remind you. It is no trouble; I was sailing this way.
The price was an axe head of silver. Now it is that and the price of my night's sleep, which I value. Or give me the skins back, and we have both had a sail.
Or run. There is shoal water under your lee and you draw less than I do. If I catch you I take the skins and leave you the boat. A story needs a living man to tell it.
Lie to and weigh out his price, with the price of his night's sleep on top
Run for shoal water, where her keel cannot follow yours
Lie to and hand it back over the gunwale

He weighs it on his own scale across two gunwales in a swell, and does not spill a penny. 'Now it is bought. Tell them on your island that Thorleif sells, and that he was not asked first.' His ship goes about and is gone before noon.

You take her in over the bank with a hand's breadth under the keel and the sounding pole going. He follows until his steersman shouts, then lies to and watches you go. He lifts one hand. You think he is laughing.

The bank is not where it was. She touches, and by the time she floats he is alongside. They take the book, a cask and a tooth from the mate, and leave the boat, as he said. 'It goes to Asulf at Sliesthorp with the next lot. Bring silver. It is easier on the hounds.'

He takes the bundle in both hands and looks into the sack to see that it is the same one. 'You came a long way to carry my goods for me.' His crew laugh; yours do not. He says it goes south to Asulf with the next lot, and that buying is permitted.
Asulf's lot
On a bench outside the dealer's pen, with a sealskin, two cups and a bell without a tongue, lies the block of calfskins. A spare, pale-eyed Svea is counting its leaves for the second time.
From Thorleif, with the autumn lot. He says a Frisian told him what it is, and to ask more than skins are worth. You are a Frisian.
From Thorleif. He says you know this piece, and the way to his bed in the dark. Here you may look at it by day.
Two hundred and fifty-eight skins. I counted two hundred and fifty-eight before. Eight ounces. Scraped clean, they will take a tally as well as new skin.
Or not scraped. I have a man at home who reads such marks. He is English. He might be worth more with something to read.
Fifteen ounces takes it now. Or two Frankish blades: a blade buys me more people than silver does. I do not haggle twice.
A Christian I may not sell south to the Franks. A Christian's book I may sell to anyone. I did not make the law. I only notice it.
Outbid the Svea: fifteen ounces, two hundred and fifty pennies' weight
Give the dealer two Frankish swords for it
Tell the Svea truly what a house of monks would give for it, and let it go east

Asulf cuts nothing from his arm ring today. The Svea closes his scales, puts them back in their bronze case, and says that he had only bid for the skins. He watches the book all the way down to your boat.

Asulf looks along each blade and sets them inside the pen door, out of the damp. The Svea counts something on his fingers and stops. The book is yours. Somewhere east of here two swords will be turned into people.

You say it plainly: its own house would give a farm for it; a king might give more. The Svea repeats this back to you slowly, and is silent, and then bids twenty ounces. Asulf takes it. 'He will hear of this in the west,' he says. 'Thorleif pays for a true word. Go and see him next summer.' The book goes into a fur bale for Birka.
Low water
You carry the bundle up from the boat over wet sand. Word has run ahead of you: the brethren are standing outside the church, and nobody speaks.
The bishop does not take it at once. He opens it where it lies in your arms, turns to one leaf and puts his little finger through the hole. 'Wigfrith,' he says. 'You careful, careful man.'
I am Ecgberht. Bishop Higbald died in May, before Whitsun, and he asked after this in his last week. Let me see the first leaf of John. Yes. He described it to me, in case.
The old brothers have told of this book since before I took vows. There should be a hole in one leaf. There is. I did not truly believe in the hole until now.
It has been in the sea. Mark has run. Well. So have we all been in the sea, these years, and we are still read from.
How did you come by it? I ask because of your face. Then there will be a sail, some morning. We know what that is. I do not say you did wrong. I say I will not be able to help you with it.
You have brought it again. Am I to look at it again, or is it staying this time?
I have nothing in my hands today but this. Come at the saint's feast in spring, or at Aidan's at the end of harvest. The estates will have sent by then, and the king's rock will have heard.
Lay it in his hands and ask nothing
Give it over, and ask back what it cost you and a fair freight
Let him see it, and carry it back to the boat: others will pay more

You put it in his hands and step back. He stands holding it as if it weighed what the altar weighs. A brother begins a psalm and the others take it up, badly, because some of them are weeping. Nobody thanks you. It does not seem to be that kind of thing. Come at the feast, the bishop says at the boat: the saint pays his own debts.

You name what it cost and what the carrying is worth, and he nods at each sum: this is a language he was afraid you might not speak. 'That is fair, and it will be paid. Come at the feast.' The book goes into the church. The brethren sing over it, and one of them brings your crew a cheese.
He closes the book himself and puts it back in your arms. 'York has silver. The Franks have more. I know what I have.' He walks you to the sand, because you are a guest. The brethren do not.
On the altar
On the feast the book lies open on the altar at the first leaf of John. The brethren from the estates are here, and a thegn from the king's rock, and a merchant who is asked to stand at the front.
The heathen men took this from us. A shipman of Dorestat went north after it and came back. I do not know that such a thing has been done before. Write the day down.
He asked nothing for it. I have told him that will not be allowed.
He asked what it cost him and a fair freight. That is a merchant's honesty, and I wish more lords had it.
It came home marked by the sea. We will not mend those leaves. Let whoever reads Mark here remember how it came back.
We saw their sails from the rock that day, and we did not come. I have brought silver. It does not mend that. I have brought it anyway.
One thing more. The saint's peace runs to the tide line. Past it there is a man with a striped sail who thinks he is owed. Pray; and keep a lookout.
Here is what we have: the silver that York collected and the king's rock has added, wax from our farms, ground on this island, and what a saint can give. Say which.
Take what he offers the giver: your name in the book of life, a cloth from the saint's coffin, and the carrying of the house's wine
Take the ransom: York's collection, the thegn's silver and the house's wax
Ask for ground instead: a boat strand and a storehouse inside the harbour sands

Your name is written among the friends of the house, to be read at the altar while the house stands. A strip of the linen that lay on Cuthbert's coffin is folded into your hand. The thegn presses his silver on you all the same, and the bishop will have his wine from no other boat. On this coast, from now on, you are Saint Cuthbert's man.

Nine hundred pennies' weight, some of it cut plate, and ten cakes of wax carried down by brothers who will not let your crew lift them. Your name goes into the book of life with the rest. It is the best freight you have ever been paid, and the bishop looks as if he thinks it cheap.

He walks the ground with you at low water: a strip above the tide inside the sands, where a boat lies easy in a west wind, and leave to build on it. A brother cuts the bounds on a stick. A Frisian has a strand on the bishop's island. The thegn says he will tell the king before the king hears it from someone else.
A house with walls
The scribe has told his lord what lies in your boat. The archbishop comes down to the staith himself, which he does not do for wine.
The island's hand, sixty or seventy years old. And there is the hole. I am sorry. I had to tell him. He is my lord, and I am fond of eating.
The island could not keep it once. It has no wall, no ditch and no spears, and the same ships are at sea this summer. Here it would lie behind stone, with the best books north of the Alps beside it.
I hear you carried it up their sand and down again. So you are a man who can be talked to.
I will pay as the island cannot. Silver, weighed here today. A clerk of mine to keep your goods and write to you by every ship. Or ground by the river, if you would rather have land than a man.
The scribe says nothing. He holds up his ink-stained thumb behind his lord's back and moves it upward, twice.
The island's bishop will write to me. He will write very well. I shall answer that the book is safe, and that is the end of what he can do.
Sell it for his first price in silver, and a clerk of the minster to keep your goods here
Name the price the scribe taught you: a herd, a year and the saint's name
Sell it for less silver and a house plot by the Ouse
Say it is not for sale here: it goes to the island

Twelve hundred pennies' weight is counted out on the staith, and a young clerk is told that he keeps a Frisian's goods from today. The book goes up to the minster under a cloth. On the island they will hear of it within the month, and they will know who sold it.

You name the herd, the year and the saint, and what each is worth, in that order. The archbishop looks at his scribe, who is looking at the river. Seventeen hundred, and the clerk. 'You have been to school,' the archbishop says. 'I wonder where.' On the island they will hear of it within the month.

Six hundred pennies' weight, and a strip of ground between the street and the Ouse with leave to build and to draw up a boat. The reeve marks the corners. The book goes up to the minster under a cloth. You have a house in the richest market of the north, and a bishop further up the coast who will not forget how you came by it.

'Then carry it carefully,' the archbishop says, 'since you carry it for nothing.' He goes back up the hill with his thegns. The scribe stays a moment and says the island has a friend he had not expected, and that there is still some of the bread left from noon.
The king's alms
A tall stooping monk in a patched cowl has been asking along the bank for a ship that goes north. He sees what you carry before you have said a word, and sits down on a mooring post.
Forgive me. I am not often short of breath on dry land. Is that from the island? May I see the first leaf of John? Only that one. Thank you. Yes.
I carry my master Alcuin's answer to the bishop. He promised to speak to King Charles for the boys who were taken, and he has spoken. I have a bag of the king's alms for ransom, and nobody to ransom.
My master has Saint Martin's at Tours now. He would have this copied before it went home, and then he would send it home. He is like that. It makes him expensive to serve.

A book is not a boy. But it was carried off by the same hands, and alms given for the one may honestly buy back the other. Let me take it north as the king's gift. You would be paid here, today, in full.
And the abbot who keeps the toll here does what my master asks. A man who brought this out of the north should not pay a tenth on this bank again. I can have that written.
I will be honest. I am a bad sailor and the book would be safer with you. But it would come to the island as your gift then, and not the king's, and kings count such things.
Give it into his hands for the king's alms: he will take it to the island as King Charles's gift
Take part of the alms toward what you paid, and Alcuin's letter, and carry the book home yourself
Let him read in it for an evening, and decide nothing

He counts out a thousand pennies as if each one hurt, and has the abbot's clerk write that your boat goes free of the toll at Quentovic. Then he wraps the book in his own cloak and goes to look for another ship north, apologising to the skipper before he has found him. The island will have its book back from the hand of the king of the Franks, and will know whom to thank.

He weighs out a hundred and fifty pennies toward the ransom and gives you his master's letter to carry with the book. 'Then it is your gift. I shall tell him so. He will be pleased, and then he will ask why I am not on your ship.' He is still explaining why not when you cast off.

He reads by a rush light at the hospice, aloud, following the line with a straw so as not to touch the skin. You follow some of it. Twice he stops to tell you that the cold on this coast gets into a man's knees. In the morning he gives the book back with both hands.
A true word
The big red-fair man sees your sail before you see him, and sends a boy down to say there is a place for you on the bench and that nobody will ask what you paid for it.
Twenty ounces, Asulf had for my box of skins. From a Svea. Nobody has had twenty ounces from a Svea since the gods were young. He says it was your word that did it.
We have met by night, you and I. This is better. There is more light, and the hounds are fed.
The woman has the round mount on her cloak still. 'He says you told the Svea what the lid was worth as well. Nobody will have that from me. It will go into the ground with me.'
The skins are at Birka. They say the Svea has an Englishman who reads them aloud to him at night. The Svea understands none of it and will not miss an evening. Explain that to me, if you can.

I pay for a true word. It is rarer than a book. Walrus tooth and a guest's seat here; or my sister's son, who has a boat and wants a partner with silver; or your share on the scale, and my steersman shows you the sound.
Take his gift of walrus tooth, and a guest's place in his hall and on his coast
Lay goods together with his sister's son, who has a boat and no silver
Take your share by weight and the marks of the sound, and carry word to the island of where its book lies

Eight tusks from the far north, each as long as your forearm, and his word before the whole bench that your sail is a guest's sail from here to the mouth of the sound. It is a strange thing to have the friendship of the man who emptied Saint Cuthbert's church. It will keep his ships off yours, and perhaps his friends' ships too.

The young man has a good boat, a quick tongue and five bundles of marten that are yours to sell for the common stock. You swear it with joined hands before the bench. In the Christian ports they will ask whose kin your partner is, and you will have to decide each time how much to say.

Six hundred pennies' weight in cut silver, and three days in his steersman's boat learning the Karmsund: the rock that shows at half tide, the two cairns in line, where the stream turns. And a thing to tell on the island: the book is whole, it is at Birka, and it is read. It is not what the bishop prays for. It is more than he has now.

A gospel book that the heathen men carried off from Saint Cuthbert's island has come home. A Frisian shipman of Dorestat found it in the north and brought it over the sand at low water. It lay on the altar at the feast.

The archbishop at Eoforwic has bought a gospel book that was taken from Saint Cuthbert's island, from a Frisian shipman who had it in the north. The island's bishop has written to ask for it. The book is in the minster.

King Charles's alms have bought back a gospel book that the heathen men took from Saint Cuthbert's island. Alcuin's monk is carrying it north. A Frisian of Dorestat found it and goes free of the toll at Quentovic for it.
They say in the north that a Svea paid twenty ounces of silver for a Christian book without its boards, on a Frisian's word of what it was worth, and took it east to Birka in a bale of furs.

A northern beach market on a grey late-summer afternoon: a dealer squats behind a cloth on the shingle with a silver cup, a small house-shaped box and a narrow strip of gilt bronze knotwork on it; a merchant's hand reaches for the strip; tents and drawn-up boats behind.

Inside the wooden church at Lindisfarne, morning light falling through the doorway where the doors have been torn off: a gaunt old bishop with a plain wooden staff counts on his raised fingers; behind him a bare altar and an empty book stand.

The minster's writing room at York on a cold bright day: a scribe at a slanted desk by a small window, pen lifted, breath showing, ruled calfskin before him and horns of red, yellow and green colour; a Frisian merchant in a short cloak waits by the door.

Evening at sea in a small open boat under a brown sail, low sun, calm water: a thin English youth holds up a wax tablet on which he has drawn a page with a small round hole in it; the steersman and the skipper lean in over their bread.

A Norse hall on a bright summer day, the door open on a sound with a ship drawn up: a big red-fair chief holds open a book without covers at a page of red, yellow and green knotwork; two hounds lie on a chest behind him; a woman at an upright loom wears a round gilt mount as a brooch.

The small boat hard pressed under a dark afternoon sky, a green sea breaking over her quarter; the skipper crouched under the tilt with a wrapped bundle held against his chest; the broad steersman braced at the steering oar, looking to windward.

Clear mid morning on a grey-blue sea, seen from the small boat's stern: a longship close astern under a red and undyed striped sail, shields along her side, a big man standing easy in the bow with one hand raised; pale shoal water to leeward.

Sliesthorp in spring under a flat white sky: a bench outside a wattle pen with a sealskin, two cups, a tongueless bell and the coverless book on it; a spare pale-eyed Svea in a fur-trimmed cap counts its leaves with one finger while a stout Dane with a plaited beard and a hazel switch watches him.

Low water at Lindisfarne, wet sand shining under a wide pale sky: a merchant walks up from a beached boat carrying a bundle in both arms; ahead, monks in undyed habits stand silent outside a wooden church with no doors, the old bishop a step in front of them.

The church at Lindisfarne on a feast day, new doors standing open, candles lit: the book open on the altar at a great decorated first letter; the bishop beside it, the brethren crowded behind, a thegn in a dark red cloak with a bag of silver, and a Frisian merchant standing at the front, ill at ease.

The river staith at York on a clear afternoon: an archbishop in a rich dark cloak, armed thegns at his back, stands over a small Frisian boat pointing at a wrapped bundle in the skipper's arms; behind him a scribe looks away at the river; the stone minster on the hill.

The river bank at Quentovic toward evening, soft light, ships moored along the timber bank: a tall stooping monk in a patched black cowl sits on a mooring post with the open book across his knees and a leather letter case under his arm, a small bag of coin on the ground at his feet.

The Norse hall at night, long fire burning, guests on the benches: the red-fair chief stands and holds out a walrus tusk to a Frisian merchant in the guest's seat; the woman beside him wears the round gilt book mount on her cloak; through the open door, the sound in the last light of a northern summer night.
